ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are two schematic diagrams, upper and lower, in the figure. In the upper figure I, the left side is wall 2, and the right side is wall 1; the left support is labeled M2, and the right support is labeled M1. Block B is located between the two springs, the spring on the left is labeled S2, and the spring on the right is labeled S1. The lower figure II shows that block B has been moved a distance x relative to the equilibrium position, in the direction toward the side of wall 1. The text of the problem gives that the stiffness coefficient of S1 is k, the stiffness coefficient of S2 is 4k, the masses of the supports and springs can be neglected, and there is no friction. Reasoning: Since M1 and M2 are not fixed on the walls, if a spring is stretched, the light support will move along with it and cannot maintain stretching by relying on the wall; therefore at the end point, only the spring on the side that is pressed toward the corresponding wall stores elastic potential energy. At the initial release, B is displaced x toward wall 1, the right-side S1 is compressed by x, and the left-side S2 actually does not store energy, so the initial elastic potential energy is (1/2)kx^2. When reaching the maximum displacement y on the other side, B is toward wall 2, the left-side S2 is compressed by y, and the right-side S1 does not store energy, so the elastic potential energy at this time is (1/2)(4k)y^2. There is no friction and the kinetic energy at the turning points is both 0, so mechanical energy is conserved: (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(4k)y^2. Solving gives x^2 = 4y^2, therefore y/x = 1/2.

raw_record.question_text: A block (B) is attached to two unstretched springs S1 and S2 with spring constants $k$ and $4k$, respectively (see figure I). The other ends are attached to identical supports M1 and M2 not attached to the walls. The springs and supports have negligible mass. There is no friction anywhere. The block B is displaced towards wall 1 by a small distance $x$ (figure II) and released. The block returns and moves a maximum distance $y$ towards wall 2. Displacements $x$ and $y$ are measured with respect to the equilibrium position of the block B. What is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$?

method.method_draft: Use a turning-point energy comparison with the movable supports. First read the diagram: in figure I the block B is between left spring S2 and right spring S1, with supports M2 and M1 adjacent to walls 2 and 1 respectively; in figure II the block is shifted toward wall 1 by distance x. From the text, S1 has spring constant k, S2 has spring constant 4k, supports/springs are massless, and there is no friction. Key bridge: because the supports are not attached to the walls, a spring cannot remain stretched by pulling on a wall support; the support would simply move, so only the spring compressed against its wall stores energy. At the initial release toward wall 1, S1 is compressed by x while S2 is effectively unstretched, so stored energy is (1/2)kx^2. At the opposite extreme toward wall 2, S2 is compressed by y while S1 is effectively unstretched, so stored energy is (1/2)(4k)y^2. Equate energies and solve: (1/2)kx^2=(1/2)(4k)y^2, giving y/x=1/2.

推理：由于 M1、M2 并未固定在墙上，弹簧若被拉伸，轻支座会随之移动，不能靠墙保持拉伸；因此在端点处只有被压向相应墙的一侧弹簧储存弹性势能。初始释放时，B 朝墙 1 位移 x，右侧 S1 被压缩 x，左侧 S2 实际不储能，所以初始弹性势能为 (1/2)kx^2。到达另一侧最大位移 y 时，B 朝墙 2，左侧 S2 被压缩 y，右侧 S1 不储能，所以此时弹性势能为 (1/2)(4k)y^2。无摩擦且转折点动能均为 0，机械能守恒： (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(4k)y^2。解得 x^2 = 4y^2，因此 y/x = 1/2。

method.method_draft: Use a piecewise SHM/velocity-at-equilibrium argument. Read the image first: the block starts in figure II displaced by x toward wall 1, so the right-side spring S1 is the compressed active spring; later the maximum y toward wall 2 corresponds to compression of the left-side spring S2. From the text, k1=k for S1 and k2=4k for S2, and the system is frictionless. Let the mass of B be m. During the first part, motion from x to equilibrium is the quarter-cycle of an oscillator with spring constant k, so the block's speed at equilibrium is v=omega1 x=sqrt(k/m)x. After crossing equilibrium toward wall 2, the active restoring spring is S2 with constant 4k, so that same speed at equilibrium corresponds to amplitude y satisfying v=omega2 y=sqrt(4k/m)y. Therefore sqrt(k/m)x=sqrt(4k/m)y, giving y/x=1/2.

ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A block (B) is attached to two unstretched springs S1 and S2 with spring constants $k$ and $4k$, respectively (see figure I). The other ends are attached to identical supports M1 and M2 not attached to the walls. The springs and supports have negligible mass. There is no friction anywhere. The block B is displaced towards wall 1 by a small distance $x$ (figure II) and released. The block returns and moves a maximum distance $y$ towards wall 2. Displacements $x$ and $y$ are measured with respect to the equilibrium position of the block B. What is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$?

The other ends are attached to identical supports M1 and M2 not attached to the walls. The springs and supports have negligible mass. There is no friction anywhere. The block B is displaced towards wall 1 by a small distance $x$ (figure II) and released. The block returns and moves a maximum distance $y$ towards wall 2. Displacements $x$ and $y$ are measured with respect to the equilibrium position of the block B. What is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$?
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: There are two schematic diagrams, upper and lower, in the figure. In the upper figure I, the left side is wall 2, and the right side is wall 1; the left support is labeled M2, and the right support is labeled M1. Block B is located between the two springs, the spring on the left is labeled S2, and the spring on the right is labeled S1. The lower figure II shows that block B has been moved a distance x relative to the equilibrium position, in the direction toward the side of wall 1. The text of the problem gives that the stiffness coefficient of S1 is k, the stiffness coefficient of S2 is 4k, the masses of the supports and springs can be neglected, and there is no friction.

Reasoning: Since M1 and M2 are not fixed on the walls, if a spring is stretched, the light support will move along with it and cannot maintain stretching by relying on the wall; therefore at the end point, only the spring on the side that is pressed toward the corresponding wall stores elastic potential energy. At the initial release, B is displaced x toward wall 1, the right-side S1 is compressed by x, and the left-side S2 actually does not store energy, so the initial elastic potential energy is (1/2)kx^2. When reaching the maximum displacement y on the other side, B is toward wall 2, the left-side S2 is compressed by y, and the right-side S1 does not store energy, so the elastic potential energy at this time is (1/2)(4k)y^2. There is no friction and the kinetic energy at the turning points is both 0, so mechanical energy is conserved: (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(4k)y^2. Solving gives x^2 = 4y^2, therefore y/x = 1/2.
